item.title: A more-than-urban political ecology approach to climate adaptation governance through the lens of infrastructures: A case in the coastal metropolitan region of Barcelona
item.description:
Júlia Mattos, Lucía Argüelles, Laura Calvet-Mir, Hug March
European Urban and Regional Studies
DOI: 10.1177/09697764261495011
In the context of the climate emergency, the increasing vulnerability of critical infrastructure has become a central socio-political condition, reshaping metropolitan governance and power relations. While critical urban studies traditionally prioritize high-density urban cores, understanding the governance dynamics in spaces of extended urbanization is increasingly vital for achieving regional climate justice. This paper departs from a more-than-urban political ecology perspective to analyze how climate-impacted infrastructures, viewed as material sites of contestation, shape metropolitan adaptation governance. Building on the politicized nature of infrastructures, we examine how grassroots actors and formal institutions negotiate the protection of two transport-related networks and the coastal defense infrastructure in El Maresme, a coastal county within Barcelona’s metropolitan region. Our research, based on non-participant field observations and semi-structured interviews with grassroots platforms and institutional actors, reveals three primary dynamics influencing the governance of climate adaptation. First, tensions among local governments arise in managing vulnerability to extreme events. Second, the climate emergency is reshaping local planning visions and future imaginaries, posing challenges to metropolitan governance. Finally, there are intensified scale-related conflicts concerning the city of Barcelona and its core metropolitan area. The study provides insights into how infrastructure mediates the relationship between grassroots movements and state responses in the context of the climate emergency. By viewing infrastructure as a diagnostic lens, we can more clearly identify the procedural injustices that characterize metropolitan adaptation governance.
